title: Primary-region evacuation stutter and degraded KV-cache reconciliation
creator: Omar Rahman
summary: A scheduled maintenance-induced region evacuation triggered an oscillating subset of circuit breakers, causing 'stutter' failovers and prolonged degraded tail latency due to KV-cache reconciliation delays. This incident caused SLO misses for the primary-region customers for ~46 minutes and observable request amplification in secondary regions.
timeline:
2026-03-09T02:05Z: Scheduled maintenance window began for primary-region (PR).
2026-03-09T02:07Z: Control plane signaled node drain for GPU-pool-a in PR.
2026-03-09T02:10Z: Traffic routed away; lightweight probe traffic started to secondary-region (SR) and warmup paths initiated.
2026-03-09T02:12Z: Intermittent KV-cache eviction spikes observed as warmup tasks raced with eviction controller.
2026-03-09T02:15Z: A subset of per-customer circuit breakers in SR tripped repeatedly (open->half-open->open) due to bursty retry traffic and TTL mismatches in priority queues.
2026-03-09T02:18Z: Routing controller attempted incremental fanout back to PR (sticky affinity), causing oscillation and amplified KV-cache warmup churn.
2026-03-09T02:35Z: SLO alert fired: 99th percentile end-to-end latency exceeded regional SLO for PR.
2026-03-09T02:47Z: Mitigation: traffic steering to a dedicated warm pool, KV-cache rate-limiter introduced, and circuit breaker hysteresis increased.
2026-03-09T02:51Z: 99th percentile latency returned within SLO bounds.
2026-03-09T03:00Z: Post-incident stabilization and manual review of reconciliation logs completed.
impact: Customer-facing SLO misses for primary-region lasting ~46 minutes (02:35–03:21 UTC window including alerts). Approximately 4% of requests experienced >5x latency at the 99th percentile. Secondary-region services experienced a 12% increase in cache-miss rate and a 7% increase in token cost due to repeated replays and retries. No data loss; no security exposure.
detection: Automated SLO alerting based on per-region 99th percentile latency and a synthetic probe suite. Observability flagged concurrent spikes in KV-cache evictions, request retries, and elevated circuit breaker open-rate metrics. Runbook was consulted at alert time but required manual tuning due to unanticipated oscillation pattern.
root_cause: Three contributing issues: 1) Race between KV-cache warmup jobs and the eviction controller under rapid route changes caused sustained cache miss amplification. 2) Circuit breakers used aggressive half-open probes with low hysteresis; when faced with bursty retries they flipped frequently, preventing stable failover. 3) Routing controller's sticky-affinity heuristic attempted incremental fanout back to primary-region during ongoing warmup, creating a feedback loop that amplified both (1) and (2).
short_term_mitigation: 1) Redirected traffic to an isolated warm pool to avoid shared eviction pressure. 2) Temporarily increased circuit breaker half-open timeout and reduced probe frequency (hysteresis). 3) Disabled incremental sticky-affinity during active warmup windows. These changes were rolled within 8 minutes of the alert and validated by synthetic probes.
long_term_fixes:
1) Implement a KV-cache warmup token-bucket limiter to throttle warmup IO and avoid eviction storms.
2) Add regional circuit-breaker mode: when a region is in evacuation or warmup state, use 'conservative' breaker settings (longer half-open, fewer probes, exponential backoff).
3) Make routing controller aware of 'warmup' state and enforce a no-incremental-fanout policy until warmup metrics (cache-hit-rate, probe-latency) reach thresholds.
4) Extend runbook with an evacuation playbook that sequences: pause warmups -> route to warm pool -> monitor cache-hit-rate -> enable incremental fanout.
5) Add a dashboard tile that correlates route changes, cache-eviction-rate, and breaker-open-rate for real-time ops decisions.

postmortem_notes: We observed an emergent feedback loop that was not covered by existing runbooks because maintenance evacuations were assumed to be low-risk for warmup eviction storms. The incident underlines that small heuristic changes (sticky-affinity increment) can interact nonlinearly with cache and breaker subsystems. Early mitigation succeeded because of fast collaboration between runtime, routing, and oncall teams.
